sum.text: Britain and India signing the landmark Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) in July went far beyond a signature. It was a chance for opportunities to be brought to life between two thriving economies. Estimated to boost bilateral trade by £25.5 bn (~₹3.26 lakh cr) every year by 2040, it's a deal that's good for British and Indian businesses, for consumers and for growth. Both Britain and India are already starting to feel the benefits, with nearly £12 bn (~₹1.53 lakh cr) worth of trade and investment deals struck since the agreement was signed, supporting thousands of jobs in both countries. This is just the beginning. India is expected to become the third largest global economy by 2031, and by 2050 is projected to be home to over a quarter of a billion high-income consumers. This means there are huge opportunities for both countries in the years ahead. Consumers in both countries are already enjoying greater access to iconic products, and we've already seen the first shipment of Scottish salmon arrive in India tariff-free via Bakkafrost Scotland. Bilateral trade is rising. British and Indian innovators are developing new technologies together with Polymateria striking a deal on their biodegradable milk pouches, now on shelves nationwide across India. Last year, UK-India Vision 2035 was signed to revitalise an already ambitious relationship, making it future-focused and ready to unlock the huge potential on offer. So, it's great to see this in action already. This partnership will deliver growth, security and opportunity for people in all corners of both countries from Merseyside to Mumbai. And our relationship extends far beyond trade. For instance, the official opening of University of Liverpool's Bengaluru campus this week, giving Indian students greater access to world-class British degrees, with 10,000 students expected to be studying there within 10 years. English Premier League is having a fantastic impact on community and grassroots football in India, with tens of millions of fans across the country. But we know there's more to do. Ministries on both sides want work with businesses, both in Britain and India, to understand how we can better support them to take advantage of what's on offer. points: India has entered a golden age of entrepreneurship, with active companies rising from 1.6 million to 2.2 million over three years.
The surge in formalisation and new businesses is driven by easing regulations and a falling cost of capital.
The reduction in India's cost of capital is underpinned by the government's progress in fiscal consolidation and low general government fiscal deficits.
A shrinking deficit constrains short-term growth, leaving India's output a year behind its pre-pandemic path and signaling slack in the job market.
To fill economic slack, the unstated policy has relied on the private sector using cheaper debt and equity capital to build businesses and create jobs.
Debt and equity financing are highly favourable, with home loan rates near 7% and stock sales by companies and promoters projected to reach nearly 6 trillion rupees this year.

sum.text: We have entered a golden age of Indian entrepreneurship. The number of active companies has risen by more than half a million in 3 years, from 1.6 mn to 2.2 mn. Many of these are new companies. At the same time, several are likely informal businesses registering formally as companies. For decades, surveys showed that barriers to formalisation were mainly a high regulatory burden (high formalisation costs), particularly for smaller firms, and limited gains from formalisation because cost and access to capital were challenges. This is changing. Irrespective of whether these are new businesses or existing businesses registering themselves, the underlying drivers are 2: easing regulations and falling cost of capital. We still need to do much more on both, and it would be unwise to assume these changes come without costs. While meaningful risks from potentially excessive deregulation may be some time away, some side effects of the falling cost of capital are visible and need to be dealt with quickly. Underlying the reduction in India's cost of capital is GoI's progress in fiscal consolidation. India is among the rare major economies where general government fiscal deficit is near pre-Covid levels. Once adjusted for the off-budget spending in that era, the actual deficit is much lower today. This comes at a cost. A shrinking deficit constrains growth. India's output remains a year behind its pre-pandemic path - better than in most economies, but still signalling slack in the job market. The shortfall is equivalent to a year's new workforce going without jobs. While rapid growth creates jobs, the larger pool of under- and unemployed workers keeps real wage growth weak for many, preventing them from feeling the benefits of growth in their standard of living. This has political implications. The wise, if unstated, policy choice has been to let the private sector fill the economic slack, using cheaper capital to build businesses and create jobs. The surge in company creation and capital formation suggests this is underway. The cost and availability of both debt and equity capital are among the most favourable ever. Self-reliance, therefore, has to mean building enough depth across technology, components, skills and supply chains to make the industry more resilient and globally competitive. India’s manufacturing expansion is significant. Module manufacturing capacity has risen from 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 228 GW of installed capacity under the ALMM framework, reflecting the rapid expansion of India’s domestic solar manufacturing base.
The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme has further encouraged investment in high-efficiency and integrated manufacturing. The ₹24,000-crore PLI programme explicitly aims to develop integrated plants, local sourcing and technological self-sufficiency. But capacity at the module end tells only part of the story.
Module capacity is currently around 6.5 times domestic cell capacity. This points to a structural imbalance- India has built substantial downstream capability, while important upstream stages remain less developed. Wafers and ingots are a case in point.
The government has acknowledged the import dependence at these stages and expanded the ALMM framework to include them from June 1, 2028. That shift is important because supply-chain resilience is ultimately about controlling the points at which a disruption can stop production. Polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells and modules are not independent businesses within the solar ecosystem.
They are sequential stages of the same manufacturing chain. The opportunity now is to connect those stages more closely. Greater integration can improve control over quality and production planning, reduce exposure to sudden changes in imported input costs and create room for Indian companies to develop process expertise and intellectual property.
The ambition should be to move from assembling products in India to building the capabilities behind those products in India. The solar industry is not standing still while India builds factories. I landed in Mumbai early on Friday. The city makes a terrible first impression. As your aircraft is about to land, it feels like it will crash into a huge slum; yet, somehow, a landing strip emerges.
There was a first-time flyer seated next to me, a scrawny guy probably headed to the Gulf, to work 14 hours and send money home. In full sleeves, blue denim trousers with some embroidery, neatly polished pointy black leather shoes and his backpack secured between his legs, he wanted to capture the landing, may be record evidence of his maiden flight. The guy’s arm suddenly jutted out towards the window from his middle seat — to record, of course.
Sadly, his Chinese smartphone’s camera could focus only on the scratches on the window. I empathised with him enough to forgive his crude behaviour — I was, after all, a first-time flyer not so long ago. So, I asked for his phone, to record a better video.
He was thankful — perhaps too innocent for fancy concepts like civic sense. But this is column material, I muttered to myself, and let it play out — just a small inconvenience for print real estate. Some get to capture the clouds — a brief happy moment in transit -— before being fedinto the meat grinder of a metropolis like Mumbai.
If you can hear the TV clearly in your bathroom, you are in Mumbai, a city where a home is a bed and a toilet, with some space to keep your shoes. Naturally, people go home in Mumbai only to sleep. That’s why there are so many thronging the streets at any given time of the day.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)'s flood forecasting section issued an alert for settlements along the river early on Sunday morning, warning of possible flooding.&nbsp; “#SMSAlert October 11, Morning 06:40.
